course.title: Academic Writing
course.description: A practical foundations course in academic writing, the formal, evidence-based prose used in essays, reports, and research. You will learn how academic writing differs from casual and creative writing, how to plan and draft an argument, how to structure essays and paragraphs, and how to use and cite sources honestly. Structure and facts adapted from Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: Academic writing is best described as...
options: formal, evidence-based, and objective in tone
a free stream of unsupported opinions
the same as a private diary entry
questions.explanation: Academic writing aims to be formal, grounded in evidence, and measured in tone rather than personal or offhand.

questions.prompt: The first stage of the writing process is usually...
options: prewriting: planning, reading, and gathering ideas
questions.explanation: Prewriting comes first - you plan, gather material, and shape ideas before drafting.

options: the opening sentence of every paragraph
a single arguable claim the whole essay supports
the last line of the conclusion
questions.explanation: A thesis is one focused, arguable claim that the rest of the essay sets out to support.

options: at the very end of the essay
at the start of a body paragraph, naming its main point
questions.explanation: A topic sentence opens a body paragraph and tells the reader what that paragraph will argue.

questions.prompt: Restating a source's idea in your own words and sentence structure is called...
questions.explanation: Paraphrase means rewording an idea in your own phrasing while still crediting the source.

questions.prompt: Presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own, without credit, is...
questions.explanation: Using another person's work without attribution is plagiarism, a serious academic offense.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a widely used citation style?
questions.explanation: MLA, along with APA and Chicago, is a standard system for formatting citations.

options: using the longest words you can find
cutting words that add no meaning
writing every paragraph as one sentence
questions.explanation: Concision is saying what you mean in as few words as needed, without padding.

lessons.title: What academic writing is, and how it differs
lessons.grammar_note: Prefer precise, measured claims over strong personal ones: write 'the evidence suggests' rather than 'I am totally sure that'.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to say what makes writing academic and to spot the differences between academic prose and other kinds of writing, such as a personal blog post, a news report, or a short story. You will learn to recognize three hallmarks that run through almost all academic work: a formal register, a reliance on evidence rather than assertion, and an objective, measured tone. Being able to name these features matters, because once you can see them you can produce them on purpose. Warm-up, drawing on the diagnostic: if a sentence reads 'This book is amazing and everyone should read it,' what two qualities of academic writing does it lack, and how might you revise it? Keep that example in mind as you read, because the rest of the lesson is really about turning instinctive, informal reactions into careful, supported statements that a reader can weigh and trust.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Academic writing is the formal style used in essays, reports, dissertations, and research articles across universities and scholarly publishing. According to Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia, it is characterized by evidence, a clear focus, and a tone that stays objective rather than emotional. Three features stand out. First, register: academic writing is formal, avoiding slang, contractions in strict contexts, and chatty asides. Second, evidence: claims are backed by data, examples, or citations rather than left as bare opinion. Third, objectivity: the writer presents arguments fairly, acknowledges other views, and hedges claims that the evidence only partly supports. This differs sharply from a diary, which is private and expressive; from journalism, which prizes speed and a broad audience; and from fiction, which invents rather than argues. Academic writing also tends to be impersonal, often favoring the subject under study over the writer's feelings. The goal is not to sound clever but to be clear, accurate, and fair so that a reader can follow and test the reasoning.

sections.heading: Techniques & examples
sections.text: Compare two versions of the same claim. Casual: 'Social media is obviously terrible for teenagers and ruins their lives.' Academic: 'Several studies report a correlation between heavy social media use and lower reported wellbeing among adolescents, though researchers caution that the direction of cause remains unclear.' Notice what changed. The sweeping word 'obviously' disappears, because academic writing earns its claims instead of asserting them. 'Terrible' and 'ruins their lives,' which are emotional and absolute, become a specific, limited statement about a correlation. A source is implied, and a qualification is added. Another example. Casual: 'I think essays are hard.' Academic: 'Students often find essay writing difficult because it requires planning, argument, and revision at the same time.' Here the vague personal feeling becomes a general, testable observation with a reason attached. The techniques are simple to practice: remove absolute words like always, never, and obviously; attach evidence or a reason to each claim; and shift from how you feel to what can be shown.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three hallmarks of academic writing introduced above. 2) Rewrite 'This theory is stupid' as an academic sentence. 3) Is a personal diary entry academic writing? Why or why not? 4) What is wrong, academically, with the word 'obviously' in a claim? 5) Which is more academic: 'Everyone knows pollution is bad' or 'Research links air pollution to higher rates of respiratory illness'? 6) Name one word, common in casual speech, that signals a claim is being asserted rather than supported. Answers: 1) Formal register, reliance on evidence, and an objective tone. 2) For example: 'This theory has been criticized because it does not account for several documented cases.' 3) No - it is private and expressive, not evidence-based or written for a critical reader. 4) It asserts that something is self-evident instead of supporting it, so it skips the evidence an academic reader expects. 5) The second, because it points to research rather than relying on an untested shared assumption. 6) Words like obviously, clearly, everyone knows, or of course all claim agreement instead of earning it with evidence.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing a formal tone with long, complicated words. Formality is about register and evidence, not about sounding grand; plain, exact words are usually better than showy ones. Mistake: thinking objectivity means you have no position. You can argue strongly for a view and still be objective, as long as you present evidence fairly and acknowledge counterarguments. Mistake: treating every personal reaction as a claim worth writing down without support. Exit ticket: (a) Name one way academic writing differs from a news article. (b) Rewrite 'Books are better than films, period' to make it more academic. Mistake: forgetting that an academic reader is a critical one who will ask for proof, not a friend who already agrees with you. Answers: (a) Academic writing cites sources and qualifies its claims, while news writing favors speed, a broad audience, and a headline-friendly summary. (b) For example: 'Compared with film adaptations, novels can offer readers more interior detail, though each form has distinct strengths, and readers value different things in each.'

lessons.title: The writing process: prewriting to editing
lessons.grammar_note: Writing is recursive, not linear: it is normal to loop back to an earlier stage, such as returning to prewriting while you revise.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: This lesson gives you a repeatable process for producing a piece of academic writing, so that a blank page stops feeling like a wall. You will be able to name and use four stages - prewriting, drafting, revising, and editing - and to explain what each stage is for and, just as important, what it is not for. Many struggling writers try to do everything at once: inventing ideas, building sentences, and fixing commas in a single pass. That overloads the mind and often stalls the work. Separating the stages lets you focus on one kind of thinking at a time. Warm-up, from the diagnostic: which stage comes first, and why would it be a mistake to start by polishing your spelling? As you read, picture a short essay you might have to write this term, and imagine moving it through each of the four stages in turn. You will also see why experienced writers treat the process as a loop rather than a straight line, returning to earlier stages whenever the work demands it, and why that flexibility is a strength rather than a sign of poor planning.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The writing process is usually described as four overlapping stages. Prewriting is everything you do before a full draft: reading, brainstorming, taking notes, narrowing a topic, and outlining. Its goal is to generate and organize ideas, not to produce finished sentences. Drafting is writing a complete version from start to finish, accepting that it will be rough; the goal is to get the whole argument down in connected prose. Revising, which literally means to see again, works at the large scale: you reconsider the thesis, the order of ideas, the strength of evidence, and whether each paragraph earns its place. Editing comes near the end and works at the small scale: sentence clarity, word choice, grammar, and punctuation. Proofreading is the final sweep for typos and formatting. These stages overlap and loop; a good writer often returns to prewriting after discovering a gap while drafting. Treating the process as recursive rather than strictly linear is one of the most useful habits a writer can build.

sections.heading: Techniques & examples
sections.text: For prewriting, try freewriting for ten minutes without stopping to generate raw material, then group related points into a rough outline. A simple outline might read: introduction with thesis; point one with evidence; point two with evidence; counterargument and response; conclusion. For drafting, follow a single rule: keep moving. If you cannot find a word, write a placeholder in brackets and continue, because stopping to perfect one sentence breaks momentum. For revising, read your draft asking big questions: Does the thesis still match what I wrote? Is each paragraph in the best order? Where is the evidence thin? It often helps to make a reverse outline, writing one sentence per paragraph to check the overall shape. For editing, read slowly, ideally aloud, to catch awkward phrasing, and check one issue at a time, such as reading once only for comma errors. Example of the payoff: a messy draft claim like '[something about cost here]' becomes, after revision and editing, 'The policy's main drawback is its high upfront cost, which smaller schools cannot absorb.'

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) List the four main stages of the writing process in order. 2) What is the single goal of the drafting stage? 3) What is the difference between revising and editing? 4) Why is it unwise to fix spelling while you are still drafting? 5) What is a reverse outline, and which stage does it help with? Answers: 1) Prewriting, drafting, revising, and editing (with proofreading as a final sweep). 2) To get the whole argument down in connected prose, accepting that it will be rough. 3) Revising reworks big-picture matters like thesis, structure, and evidence; editing fixes small-scale matters like grammar, word choice, and punctuation. 4) It splits your attention and interrupts momentum, and you may delete the very sentences you were polishing. 5) A reverse outline summarizes each finished paragraph in one sentence to reveal the draft's real structure; it helps most with revising. 6) True or false: a good writer produces a clean, final piece in a single pass. False - almost all strong writing moves through several drafts, which is exactly why the staged process exists.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: skipping prewriting and starting a draft with no plan, which usually produces a shapeless piece that needs heavy rebuilding later. Mistake: editing too early, so you polish sentences that revision will later cut. Mistake: treating the first draft as the final draft; almost no strong writing survives without revision. Mistake: believing good writers produce clean prose in one pass - most do not, and the process exists precisely because they do not. Exit ticket: (a) Which stage is for generating and organizing ideas? (b) You notice your whole second section is in the wrong place. Is that a revising task or an editing task? Mistake: expecting the stages to run in a tidy straight line, when in practice you often loop back, for example returning to prewriting after a draft reveals a gap in your evidence. Answers: (a) Prewriting. (b) Revising, because moving a whole section is a large-scale, structural change rather than a small sentence-level fix.

lessons.title: Thesis statements and building an argument
lessons.grammar_note: A thesis should be a claim someone could reasonably disagree with; if no one could argue the other side, it is a fact or a topic, not a thesis.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: After this lesson you will be able to write a clear, arguable thesis statement and to build an argument that supports it. The thesis is the backbone of an academic essay: it tells the reader what you claim and promises what the rest of the piece will show. Many weak essays are weak not because the sentences are poor but because there is no single controlling claim, so the writing wanders. You will learn to tell a thesis apart from a topic and from a plain fact, and to test whether a thesis is specific and arguable enough to carry an essay. Warm-up, from the diagnostic: is 'the history of coffee' a thesis? If not, what is missing, and how could you turn that topic into a claim? As you read, keep a topic you care about in mind, and try drafting a one-sentence claim about it that someone could reasonably dispute.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A thesis statement is a single sentence, usually near the end of the introduction, that states the central, arguable claim of the essay. A good thesis has three qualities. It is arguable: a reasonable person could disagree, which rules out bare facts like 'water is made of hydrogen and oxygen.' It is specific: it names a clear position rather than a broad subject, so 'social media harms teenage sleep by delaying bedtimes' beats 'social media is bad.' And it is supportable: you can defend it with the evidence available to you. An argument is the structured case for the thesis. It is built from reasons, each a sub-claim that supports the thesis, and evidence, the facts, examples, data, or expert testimony that back each reason. Strong arguments also anticipate objections and answer them, a move called addressing the counterargument. The thesis and the body work together: the thesis makes a promise, and each body paragraph delivers part of it.

sections.heading: Techniques & examples
sections.text: To sharpen a thesis, run it through a test: Could someone argue the opposite? Topic: 'remote work.' Weak thesis: 'Remote work is interesting.' Stronger: 'Remote work raises individual productivity but weakens the informal collaboration that drives long-term innovation.' That version is arguable, specific, and points toward a two-part structure. To build the argument, list the reasons that support the claim, then attach evidence to each. Reason one: focused tasks improve at home - evidence: studies showing fewer interruptions. Reason two: spontaneous idea-sharing declines - evidence: surveys on reduced cross-team contact. Then add a counterargument: some firms report strong innovation while remote, and a response: those firms often invest heavily in deliberate virtual contact. A simple template helps: 'Although [opposing view], [your claim], because [main reason].' Example: 'Although remote work boosts short-term output, it can slow innovation, because the chance encounters that spark new ideas happen less often.' This single sentence already contains a position, a concession, and a reason.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three qualities of a strong thesis. 2) Is 'The French Revolution began in 1789' a thesis? Why or why not? 3) Turn the topic 'homework' into an arguable thesis. 4) In an argument, what is the difference between a reason and evidence? 5) Complete the template: 'Although video games can be distracting, ____, because ____.' 6) Why does a thesis that no one could dispute fail as a thesis? Answers: 1) It is arguable, specific, and supportable. 2) No - it is a verifiable fact that no one disputes, so it is not arguable. 3) For example: 'Daily homework in primary school offers little academic benefit and reduces time for play that supports development.' 4) A reason is a sub-claim that supports the thesis; evidence is the facts, data, or examples that back the reason. 5) For example: '...they can also build problem-solving skills, because many games require planning and quick strategic decisions.' 6) If no reasonable person could take the other side, there is nothing to argue, so the essay can only describe or report rather than make a case.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: offering a topic instead of a thesis, so the essay describes rather than argues. Mistake: writing a thesis so broad that no essay could support it, such as 'technology has changed the world.' Mistake: stating a claim but never giving reasons or evidence, leaving the reader with an assertion. Mistake: ignoring the other side; a thesis looks stronger, not weaker, when you address the best objection to it. Exit ticket: (a) Where in an essay does the thesis usually appear? (b) Why does addressing a counterargument strengthen your case rather than undermine it? Mistake: packing two or three separate claims into one overloaded thesis, so the essay cannot deliver on all of them clearly. Answers: (a) Near the end of the introduction. (b) It shows you have considered opposing views and can answer them, which makes your position more credible and your reasoning more complete.

questions.prompt: The tone expected in most academic writing is...
questions.explanation: Academic writing stays objective and formal, presenting evidence fairly rather than leaning on feelings.

questions.prompt: During the drafting stage, your main goal is to...
options: get the whole argument down in connected prose
questions.explanation: Drafting is about producing a complete, rough version; small fixes belong to editing.
A thesis states a specific position that a reasonable person could dispute and that you can support.

questions.prompt: In a standard essay, the introduction should...
options: introduce the topic and present the thesis
questions.explanation: The introduction orients the reader to the topic and ends with the controlling thesis.

questions.prompt: Revising differs from editing because revising focuses on...
questions.explanation: Revising reworks large-scale matters; editing handles small-scale sentence and grammar fixes.

questions.prompt: Which move tends to make an argument more convincing, not less?
options: addressing a counterargument and answering it
questions.explanation: Raising and answering the strongest objection shows thoroughness and builds the reader's trust.

lessons.title: Structuring an essay
lessons.grammar_note: Think of an essay as a promise and its delivery: the introduction promises, the body delivers, and the conclusion reports back on what was shown.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: This lesson gives you a reliable shape for an academic essay, so you always know where each part of your thinking belongs. You will be able to describe the roles of the introduction, the body paragraphs, and the conclusion, and to write topic sentences that open each body paragraph with a clear claim. Structure is not a cage; it is scaffolding that frees you to concentrate on ideas, because you are not reinventing the form each time. Readers also rely on a familiar shape to follow a complex argument. Warm-up, from earlier lessons: if the thesis belongs at the end of the introduction, what job is left for the body paragraphs and the conclusion? As you read, imagine an essay with a three-part thesis and sketch how many body paragraphs it would need and what each would argue. Keep in mind that structure is a tool for the reader as much as for you: a clear shape lets someone follow a demanding argument without getting lost, and it makes gaps in your own reasoning easier to spot before a reader finds them.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A standard academic essay has three parts. The introduction orients the reader: it opens with context or a hook, narrows to the specific topic, and ends with the thesis, the controlling claim. The body is the heart of the essay, made of paragraphs that each develop one reason supporting the thesis. A typical body paragraph follows a clear pattern: a topic sentence states the paragraph's main point, evidence and explanation support it, and a final sentence links back to the thesis or forward to the next idea. The number of body paragraphs depends on how many reasons your thesis requires, not on a fixed rule like five. The conclusion does not simply repeat the introduction; it synthesizes, restating the thesis in fresh words, drawing the reasons together, and pointing to why the argument matters or what follows from it. Good structure makes the logic visible, so a reader can see how each part contributes to the whole.

sections.heading: Techniques & examples
sections.text: Build the body from your reasons. If your thesis is 'remote work raises output but weakens innovation,' you might write one paragraph on output and one on innovation, each opening with a topic sentence. A strong topic sentence makes a claim, not an announcement: write 'Working from home reduces the interruptions that fragment deep work' rather than 'This paragraph is about working from home.' Inside the paragraph, use a simple sequence: claim, evidence, explanation of how the evidence supports the claim, then a link. For the introduction, move from general to specific like a funnel: a broad opening, then the narrowed topic, then the thesis. For the conclusion, avoid adding brand-new evidence; instead, answer the question 'so what?' Example conclusion opening: 'Taken together, these findings suggest that the benefits of remote work depend less on where people sit than on how deliberately organizations design moments for contact.' That sentence restates the claim in new words and gestures at significance.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What three jobs does an introduction do? 2) Where in a body paragraph does the topic sentence usually go? 3) Rewrite this weak topic sentence as a claim: 'This paragraph talks about pollution.' 4) Should a conclusion introduce new evidence? Why or why not? 5) How do you decide how many body paragraphs an essay needs? Answers: 1) It gives context or a hook, narrows to the topic, and ends with the thesis. 2) At the start of the paragraph. 3) For example: 'Air pollution imposes measurable costs on public health, especially in dense cities.' 4) No - the conclusion should synthesize and interpret what has already been shown; new evidence belongs in the body. 5) By the number of distinct reasons your thesis requires, giving each its own paragraph, rather than following a fixed count. 6) What question should a strong conclusion answer for the reader? It should answer 'so what?' - explaining why the argument matters or what follows from it, rather than simply repeating the opening.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: writing topic sentences that announce a subject ('Now I will discuss X') instead of making a claim about it. Mistake: cramming several unrelated reasons into one giant paragraph, which buries the logic. Mistake: a conclusion that only repeats the introduction word for word, adding no synthesis. Mistake: forcing the argument into exactly five paragraphs when it needs more or fewer. Exit ticket: (a) What is the main difference between a topic sentence and a thesis? (b) Name one thing a conclusion should do besides restate the thesis. Mistake: ending a body paragraph without linking it back to the thesis, so the reader loses sight of why the paragraph is there. Answers: (a) A thesis is the single controlling claim for the whole essay; a topic sentence is the controlling claim for one paragraph. (b) It should synthesize the reasons and explain why the argument matters, or what follows from it.

lessons.title: Paragraph unity and cohesion
lessons.grammar_note: Unity is about one idea per paragraph; cohesion is about the links between sentences. A paragraph can be unified yet still read as a list of disconnected lines.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: This lesson zooms in from the whole essay to the single paragraph and the links between sentences. You will be able to write paragraphs that have unity, meaning every sentence serves one central idea, and cohesion, meaning the sentences connect smoothly so the reader never has to guess how one thought relates to the next. These two qualities are often confused but are not the same: a paragraph can stick to one topic yet still feel choppy, and a paragraph can flow nicely yet wander off topic. Warm-up, from the last lesson: if a topic sentence states a paragraph's main claim, what should happen to a sentence in that paragraph that does not relate to the claim? As you read, keep in mind a paragraph you have written that felt disjointed, and watch for the specific tools that would have tied it together. By the end you will have a short checklist you can run over any paragraph to test both qualities at once, which is far faster than rereading a whole essay hoping the problems jump out at you.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Unity means a paragraph develops a single controlling idea, usually named in its topic sentence. Every other sentence should support, explain, or illustrate that idea; anything that does not belong is cut or moved. Cohesion means the sentences hang together, so the reader feels a smooth flow rather than a pile of separate statements. Writers build cohesion with several tools. Transition words and phrases, such as however, therefore, for example, and in contrast, signal the logical relationship between ideas. Repeating a key term, or using a pronoun that clearly points back, keeps the subject in view. The old-to-new principle helps too: begin a sentence with information the reader already has, then add the new point, so each sentence hooks onto the one before. Together, unity and cohesion make a paragraph feel like a single, connected thought rather than a scattered collection of facts, and they are among the clearest signs of controlled, readable prose.

sections.heading: Techniques & examples
sections.text: Consider a choppy paragraph: 'The city built a new bike lane. Cycling increased. There were fewer car accidents. Air quality was measured. It improved slightly.' Each sentence is fine, but the links are missing. A cohesive revision: 'After the city built a new bike lane, cycling increased noticeably. As more residents rode instead of drove, the number of car accidents fell. Air quality, measured over the following year, also improved slightly.' The revision adds transitions (after, as, also), carries ideas forward with old-to-new phrasing, and keeps one subject in view. For unity, apply the topic-sentence test: cross out any sentence that does not support the paragraph's main claim. If a strong sentence does not fit, it probably belongs in another paragraph. A useful habit is to reread each paragraph and ask two questions in order: Is every sentence about the same idea? And does each sentence connect clearly to the one before it?

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Define unity and cohesion in your own words. 2) Name three transition words and the relationship each signals. 3) A paragraph on the causes of a war suddenly includes a sentence about the writer's favorite film. What principle does that break? 4) What does the old-to-new principle mean? 5) If a sentence is well written but does not fit the paragraph's main idea, what should you do with it? Answers: 1) Unity means every sentence serves one central idea; cohesion means the sentences connect smoothly. 2) For example: however (contrast), therefore (result), for example (illustration). 3) Unity, because the sentence does not serve the paragraph's controlling idea. 4) Each sentence should start with familiar information and then introduce the new point, linking it to what came before. 5) Cut it or move it to a paragraph where it fits, rather than leaving it to break unity. 6) Which quality would adding the phrase 'as a result' at the start of a sentence most help, unity or cohesion? Cohesion, because the phrase signals the logical link between that sentence and the one before it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: stuffing transition words into every sentence, which feels mechanical; use them where the logic actually needs signaling. Mistake: assuming a shared topic alone creates flow - without links, sentences still read as a list. Mistake: keeping a clever sentence that strays from the main idea just because you like it. Mistake: starting each sentence with brand-new information, forcing the reader to work out the connection. Exit ticket: (a) A paragraph stays on one idea but reads as a choppy list of facts. Which quality is missing? (b) Give one tool for improving that quality. Mistake: relying on a pronoun like 'it' or 'this' when the reader cannot tell what the pronoun points back to, which quietly breaks cohesion. Answers: (a) Cohesion is missing; unity is present. (b) Any of: transition words, repeating a key term, clear pronoun reference, or the old-to-new ordering of information.

lessons.title: Using sources and avoiding plagiarism
lessons.grammar_note: Change the words but not the credit: a paraphrase still names its source. Rewording without citing is still plagiarism.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: This lesson teaches you how to bring other people's ideas into your writing honestly and effectively. You will be able to use the three main ways of drawing on a source - summary, paraphrase, and direct quotation - and to explain when each is the right choice. You will also be able to define plagiarism and describe the habits that keep you clear of it. Integrating sources well is central to academic writing, because scholarship builds on earlier work; the point is to join a conversation, not to copy from it. Warm-up, from the diagnostic: what is the difference between paraphrasing a source and plagiarizing it? As you read, picture a paragraph of a source you admire, and think about how you would restate its main point in your own words while still giving the original author credit. This skill is one of the highest-stakes in academic writing: handled well, it shows you can engage seriously with other scholars, but handled carelessly it can sink an otherwise strong paper, so it is worth slowing down and getting the habits right from the start.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: There are three main ways to use a source. A summary condenses a long passage or a whole work into a short statement of its main points, in your own words. A paraphrase restates a specific idea in your own words and sentence structure, usually at about the same length as the original. A direct quotation reproduces the source's exact words inside quotation marks. All three require a citation that credits the source; changing the wording does not remove the duty to credit. Plagiarism is presenting someone else's words, ideas, or structure as your own without proper attribution. It includes copying text, paraphrasing too closely while swapping a few words, and even reusing your own earlier work without disclosure, known as self-plagiarism. Plagiarism can be deliberate or accidental, but both are treated seriously because academic writing depends on trust. Integrating a source well means more than inserting a quotation: you introduce it, present it accurately, and then explain how it supports your own point.

sections.heading: Techniques & examples
sections.text: Choose the method by purpose. Summarize when you need the gist of a large work. Paraphrase when you want a specific idea in your own voice, which is the most common choice in academic writing. Quote directly only when the exact wording matters - a precise definition, a memorable phrase, or language you will analyze. To paraphrase safely, read the passage, look away, and write the idea from memory, then check that both the words and the sentence pattern are genuinely yours; swapping a few synonyms while keeping the original structure is still plagiarism. Integrate quotations with a signal phrase rather than dropping them in bare. Weak: 'Cities are changing. Remote work reshapes where people live.' Stronger: 'As one analyst notes, remote work is reshaping where people choose to live, loosening the old tie between home and office.' The strong version names a source, blends the borrowing into the sentence, and sets up your own comment. Keep careful notes while researching, marking which words are the source's and which are yours, so you never lose track later.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three main ways to use a source. 2) Which method keeps the source's exact words? 3) You reword a sentence but keep its structure and give no citation. Is that acceptable? 4) When is direct quotation the best choice? 5) What is a signal phrase, and why use one? Answers: 1) Summary, paraphrase, and direct quotation. 2) Direct quotation. 3) No - a paraphrase must use your own words and structure and must still cite the source; close rewording without credit is plagiarism. 4) When the exact wording matters, such as a precise definition, a striking phrase, or language you plan to analyze. 5) A signal phrase introduces a borrowed idea (for example, 'as the author argues'); it tells the reader a source is coming and blends the quotation smoothly into your sentence. 6) Why keep careful notes marking which words are yours and which are the source's? Because weeks later it is easy to forget the origin of a sentence, and unmarked borrowing can turn into accidental plagiarism.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: patchwriting, which means paraphrasing by swapping a few synonyms while keeping the original sentence shape - it still counts as plagiarism. Mistake: dropping a quotation into a paragraph with no introduction or follow-up, so the reader cannot see why it is there. Mistake: forgetting to cite a paraphrase because the words are now yours; the idea still is not. Mistake: losing track in your notes of which words came from a source. Exit ticket: (a) Define plagiarism in one sentence. (b) You found a perfect idea in a source and restated it fully in your own words. Do you still need a citation? Mistake: quoting so heavily that your own voice disappears, leaving a paper stitched together from other people's sentences rather than your argument. Answers: (a) Plagiarism is presenting another person's words, ideas, or structure as your own without proper attribution. (b) Yes - the wording is yours, but the idea is borrowed, so the source must be credited.

lessons.title: Citation styles and clear academic style
lessons.grammar_note: Pick one citation style and stay consistent throughout a paper; mixing MLA, APA, and Chicago in a single document signals carelessness.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: This lesson covers two practical skills that polish an academic paper: citing sources in a recognized style, and writing with clarity and concision. You will be able to name three widely used citation styles - MLA, APA, and Chicago - describe where each is common, and explain why citing matters at all. You will also be able to tighten your own prose by cutting wordiness and choosing precise, plain words over vague or inflated ones. These skills come near the end of the writing process, but they shape how seriously a reader takes your work. Warm-up, from the previous lesson: if every borrowed idea needs credit, what does a reader gain from the citation you provide? As you read, keep a sentence of your own writing in mind and look for words you could remove without losing any meaning. These two skills reward each other: a correctly cited paper earns trust, and clear, concise prose makes that trust easy to keep, because the reader can follow your reasoning without fighting through clutter or wondering where a claim came from.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A citation style is an agreed set of rules for formatting references and in-text credits so that readers can identify and find your sources. Three dominate. MLA, from the Modern Language Association, is common in the humanities, especially literature and languages. APA, from the American Psychological Association, is standard in the social sciences and emphasizes dates, since recency matters there. Chicago, with its two systems of notes-bibliography and author-date, is widely used in history and publishing. They differ in surface details - how authors are listed, where the year goes, whether footnotes are used - but share a purpose. Citing matters for three reasons: it gives credit and so avoids plagiarism; it lets readers verify and follow up your evidence; and it shows you have engaged with existing work. Clarity and concision are the companion virtues of style. Clarity means a reader understands a sentence on the first pass; concision means no word is wasted. Both serve the same goal: letting the idea reach the reader with as little friction as possible.

sections.heading: Techniques & examples
sections.text: You do not need to memorize every rule of a citation style; you need to pick the one your field or instructor requires and apply it consistently, using a style guide or reference tool to check details. The key discipline is consistency within a single paper. For clarity and concision, a few moves do most of the work. Cut empty fillers: 'due to the fact that' becomes 'because,' and 'in order to' becomes 'to.' Prefer the active voice when it is clearer: 'researchers collected the data' reads better than 'the data were collected by researchers.' Replace vague words with exact ones: 'the results were affected a lot' becomes 'the results fell by nearly a third.' Watch for nominalizations, where a strong verb is buried in a noun: 'make a decision' becomes 'decide,' and 'conduct an investigation of' becomes 'investigate.' Example: the bloated sentence 'It is important to note that, in the majority of cases, the policy had a positive effect' tightens to 'In most cases, the policy helped.' Same meaning, half the words, and clearer.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name three widely used citation styles and one field each is common in. 2) Give two reasons citing sources matters. 3) Tighten this sentence: 'Due to the fact that it was raining, we made the decision to cancel the event.' 4) Rewrite in the active voice: 'The experiment was designed by the students.' 5) What is a nominalization, and why avoid overusing it? Answers: 1) MLA (humanities and literature), APA (social sciences), Chicago (history and publishing). 2) Any two of: it credits others and avoids plagiarism; it lets readers verify and follow up evidence; it shows engagement with existing work. 3) For example: 'Because it was raining, we canceled the event.' 4) 'The students designed the experiment.' 5) A nominalization turns a verb into a noun, such as 'make a decision' for 'decide'; overusing it makes prose wordy and flat, hiding the real action. 6) Why does consistency matter more than memorizing every rule of a citation style? Because you can always look up a detail in a style guide, but a paper that mixes formats looks careless and makes sources harder to trace.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: mixing citation styles within one paper, or inventing your own format; readers and graders expect a single consistent system. Mistake: believing fancy, long words make writing sound smart - they usually make it harder to read. Mistake: overusing the passive voice so that no one seems to do anything in your sentences. Mistake: leaving in filler phrases like 'it is important to note that' that add length but no meaning. Exit ticket: (a) Which citation style is most associated with the social sciences? (b) Rewrite concisely: 'At this point in time, we are in the process of conducting a review.' Answers: (a) APA. (b) For example: 'We are reviewing it now,' or 'We are now conducting a review.'

items.translation: the single, arguable claim that an essay sets out to support, usually stated at the end of the introduction
items.example: Her thesis statement promised to show that the reform helped small farms but hurt large ones.

items.translation: the sentence, usually first in a body paragraph, that states that paragraph's main point
items.example: Each body paragraph opened with a clear topic sentence before giving evidence.

items.translation: a restatement of a source's idea in your own words and sentence structure, still credited to the source
items.example: Rather than quote the whole page, he wrote a paraphrase and added a citation.

items.translation: presenting another person's words, ideas, or structure as your own without proper attribution
items.example: Swapping a few synonyms while keeping the original sentence is still plagiarism.

items.translation: a formatted credit that identifies a source so readers can find and verify it
items.example: A citation in the social sciences typically places the publication year right after the author's name.

items.translation: the quality of sentences connecting smoothly, so a paragraph reads as one linked thought
items.example: Adding transition words and repeating a key term gave the paragraph cohesion.

items.translation: saying what you mean in as few words as the meaning needs, without padding
items.example: Editing for concision turned a twenty-word sentence into a crisp ten-word one.

items.translation: a measured, fair stance that presents evidence and other views rather than personal feeling
items.example: The reviewer praised the essay's objectivity, noting that it answered the strongest counterargument.
